title: Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag)
description: Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in a single pass with three pointers and no extra memory.

data.text: Given an array `nums` containing only `0`, `1`, and `2`, sort it **in place** in a single pass without using a library sort.
Count how many of each value exist, then rewrite the array. Two passes, O(n) time, but it generalises poorly and touches the data twice.

data.title: Counting Sort O(n), two passes

data.text: Maintain three regions: `[0, low)` is all 0s, `[low, mid)` is all 1s, and `(high, n)` is all 2s. The unknown region is `[mid, high]`. Inspect `nums[mid]` and move it into the correct region, then continue. Each element is moved at most once, so it is a true single pass.

data.title: Dutch National Flag O(n), one pass
data.content: Three regions, one inspection per element.

data.title: The one rule people get wrong
data.text: When you swap with `high`, do **not** increment `mid`. The element that just arrived from the end has not been inspected yet, and it may itself be a 0 or a 2. When you swap with `low`, you *do* advance `mid`, because the element arriving from `low` is a known 1.

data.title: Why this is the real answer
data.text: This is the partition step of quicksort with two pivot values instead of one. The same three-way partition is how you handle arrays with many duplicate keys efficiently, which is exactly why quicksort implementations have a three-way variant.

data.caption: Three regions shrink the unknown middle until it is empty; each element is classified exactly once.

cards.title: Counting sort
cons: Only works for small value ranges

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: The three regions are the invariant to state out loud in an interview: everything left of `low` is 0, everything between `low` and `mid` is 1, everything right of `high` is 2, and `[mid, high]` is unexamined.
